newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's ACCC proposes new consumer body.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's ACCC proposes new consumer body.

text.p: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), the national consumer watchdog, said on Thursday it had proposed the development of a new consumer protection system in its submission to the Wallis Inquiry into the nation's financial system.

"The system would involve existing industry complaints handling and dispute resolution schemes being brought under an umbrella body responsible for all facets of the provision of consumer protection in financial services," the ACCC said.
ACCC said it also proposed the creation of a new small statutory body to harmonise and assess industry schemes.

The commission said the industry-based component of the scheme would cover accreditation, compliance, complaints handling and public education. It would also be subject to oversight and audit by a small, independent body within the treasury portfolio, the commission said.

"The statutory body would be responsible for setting policy in the financial services sector, conduct audits of the industry-based component and compliance inspections of individual financial service providers," the ACCC said.

The ACCC said this system would leverage off the good faith shown by the financial services sector in establishing complaints handling and dispute resolution schemes and in developing codes of conduct.
"It would also incorporate an appropriate level of audit and oversight to ensure a high level of consumer protection is achieved, with minimum government intervention," the ACCC said.
In the submission the ACCC said it saw a pro-competitive advantage in bringing banks, building societies, credit unions and friendly societies under a single prudential regime.
The Trade Practices Act was a crucial piece of consumer protection law and its universal application was paramount to consumer protection in financial services, the ACCC said.
"The ACCC would be strongly opposed to any proposal that the financial services sector be cosseted from competition and consumer protection laws," the commission said.

The ACCC said its submission argued for the retention of the misleading and deceptive conduct provisions of the Trade Practices Act as probably the most imporatant provision with regard to the protection of financial services users.

"The administration of the misleading and deceptive conduct provisions by the ACCC not only protects consumers but assists business by sanctioning providers whose conduct is unethical," the ACCC said.

The commission said it reiterated its view that mergers in the financial services sector should continue to be covered by the substantial lessening of competition (mergers) test and that it would continue to assess mergers on a case by case basis.
